column15: `x in set` is O(1), but `x in list` is O(n). The same code with a list would quietly become O(n^2).

column7: Hash map of complements (value -> index), one pass
column15: check BEFORE adding. That stops a number pairing with itself ([3, 2, 4], 6), and duplicates like [3, 3] still work.

column7: Two pointers converging from both ends
column15: in-place means mutate the list you were given. `s = s[::-1]` only rebinds the local name, so the caller's list never changes.

column7: Two pointers, same direction (slow writer i, fast reader j)
column15: only the first k slots are checked, so never move duplicates out. Copy each new unique value in at i + 1 and ignore the rest.

column7: Two pointers, same direction (slow writer i, fast reader j), same as LC 26
column15: never move the vals anywhere. Copy every keeper into slot i; the leftovers past k are ignored. i ends up equal to k. vs LC 26: j starts at 0, not 1, because nums[0] may itself be val. The write rule is "nums[j] != val" instead of "nums[j] != nums[i]".

column4: Best Time to Buy and Sell Stock
column7: One pass with a running minimum ("best thing seen so far")
column15: the i pointer from the brute force becomes one variable, cheapest_price. Two independent checks per day: is today the new cheapest? does selling today beat the best profit?

column7: Two pointers, one per sorted input (the "merge" step of merge sort)
column15: exactly ONE value is taken per pass, so it is if/else (unlike LC 121, where both checks could fire on the same day).

column7: Boyer-Moore voting (cancel pairs); hash-map counting as the O(n)-space step
column15: pair each vote for the leader with one vote against and drop both. A value with more than n/2 votes can't be fully cancelled, so the survivor is the winner. The vote that empties the stage is used up; the NEXT vote takes it.
